newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Pilkington sees German job cuts.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Pilkington sees German job cuts.

text.p: Pilkington Plc said on Tuesday it planned "significant" job cuts in Germany, on top of those already announced, under plans for plant closures following a profit warning earlier.

Andrew Robb, group finance director, told Reuters in an interview that Pilkington was in talks with unions in Germany about the closure of processing and double glazing plants there. "Quite a number of plants will be taken out," he said. "In Germany there will be a significant number of job losses." Pilkington has 9,000 employees in Germany.
Germany is one of the biggest markets for Pilkington glass and is also a major production base for the group.
Pilkington announced earlier that profits for the year to March 31 1997 would be well below market estimates, hitting 130 million stg before tax and exceptional charges.

This compares to a concensus market forecast of 178 million stg. The group blamed poor market conditions in Europe, particularly Germany, and the failure to make recent float glass prices stick. Another key factor blamed was the strong sterling level.
Robb said "Primarily it has been the European market conditions and glass prices. Sterling has cost us around 10 million (stg off pre-tax profits) this year."

The German market has been the biggest problem. Robb said there had been a significant fall in building products. The group hoped that by launching new price rises of "at least 20 percent" it would be able to make some of that stick. "I would expect at least half of the price rise to stick," he told Reuters.

Europe is the biggest market for the building material glass products, with sales accounting for 1.1 billion stg a year. Of that, 800 million is for continental Europe of which Germany is the biggest market. Separate from this market is the automotive glass market.

Robb said there was roughly 10 percent overcapacity in building products glass which was exacerbated by the winter slowdown in construction, but he predicted a pick-up in sales with the advent of summer weather. Closure of German plants was one way of reducing some capacity, he said.
Pilkington's Robb also said he did not anticipate further charges to profits for the year to March 31 1998, apart from on-going redundancy costs.
But he said that analysts were likely to have to pull back profit forecasts for next year. The consensus profit forecast for next year was 211.5 million stg.
On the dividend outlook, he said "Our dividend policy hasn't changed and the cash flow of the company still remains strong."
